commentBody: Not a fan usually of rebuses, but this was pleasant and nicely clued. Thanks!
A Monday puzzle with rebuses!
Another fairly straightforward day of clues. Even the rebuses weren’t that tricky by NYT Thursday standards. Not that I’m complaining. It was enjoyable.
Put me down for 350+ comments today. Rebus.
Another Thursday puzzle like having some potato chips. Just plain potato chips. No good French onion dip. A little bit of fun before bed.
Acceptable puzzle. While the crosses made it easy to get the gathering clouds answer, I think that nebulous clue would have been just about impossible to figure out.

Nice to see Maurice Ravel represented in this puzzle. If you have 13 minutes to spare, I recommend listening to this recording of “La Valse,” conducted by Leonard Bernstein. It’s quite an experience - gorgeous, elegant, magical, and dark all at once. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fg2i2NB-i3o

What I most enjoyed, after completing the puzzle, was seeing the double set of staircases in the grid, with the L-shape below "Fall" tumbling down the stairs and lying in a bent, supine position at the bottom, buττ up against "Legumes," which the poor fellow might end up being after a fall like that, a vegetable, and not of the vegan kind either! OK, after that flight (down the stairs) of fancy, I thought this was fun, had a great revealer, and a couple decent clues. Some of the clues/answers were so old hat, like the "ET TU" one, that I kept thinking, especially in the SW, that this was a section of the board I'd want to zhuzh up a bit. Like it would have been more clever to clue it as [Gay writer] than [Writer Gay]. That kind of thing. 

I know, don't tell me: like I could do any better. I can't. I'm just letting perfection be the enemy of the really good.

What way is "Gaia/Gaea" going to be spelt tomorrow?

Guya?  Gia?  Giaw?  Gieia?

I hope those who dislike rebuses will use this as a good introduction. Should be very straightforward with the clues provided and a solid revealer and fill. Not too many STUMBLINGBLOCKS but pleasant enough. Thanks Jill! My latest Crosshare puzzle just got posted. Fair Warning: this is the most intricate and jam-packed theme I ever attempted, and probably a tough solve. I didn't hold back on the clues although I hope they are fair. Also, one of the themed entries has an obvious inconsistency; I decided it was necessary to pull it all together. Also, I fixed a somewhat confusing clue thanks to Peaty & Oaty’s suggestiion—thanks! Was it all worth it? Only you can say. Good luck, you may need it! https://crosshare.org/crosswords/aZocM5ah4602fW8EkF5Y/guys-n-dolls

This is one of my favorite rebus puzzles we have had.  Still had some trouble in the west, really learned a couple of new words. 

Well done! Thank you! Add this to the list of OPUSES. or should if be opi?

The last couple of years have been rife with various health issues, not the least of which is the severe, unexplainable, systemic nerve pain I started experiencing out of the blue... it led to a bit more than a handful of nasty FALLs, SLIPs, and TRIPs (nothing broken), which did nothing to help the situation, as I'm sure you can imagine.

So this puzzle could have been a very unpleasant experience for me. Instead, it made me (again) feel so grateful that I seem to have turned a corner—without falling, no less, har—over these last four or so months. Apparently, the nerve issue is not reversible, but we're working on it being manageable. 

And... if it hadn't made me feel grateful, I'd have most likely laughed about it with dark humor! One of my favorite things during the extreme pain episodes, was my husband saying that he is amazed that I keep such good humor (even when a bit dark) throughout this horrid ordeal. Well, laugh or cry, right?!.... or why choose?! There's a time and place for each, but mostly I prefer the laughing. 

So thank you to Ms. Singer for a puzzle that made me smile despite my actual STUMBLINGBLOCKS! I do love a good rebus puzzle, and this one was definitely a good one, I thought!  Fun, revealing revealer, and not too challenging, hopefully, for newer solvers. 

Cheers all! 

P.S. We've watched all of Vera, so my first answer for 46A "Term of endearment in the U.K.) was pet, instead of LUV. ☺️

A sad coincidence. Today's NYT has a story about a German city voting to stop the installation of 'stumbling stones' as memorials in front of the homes of Jews and others murdered by the Nazis. I had heard of this practice but was unfamiliar with the name for the stones. Read all about it here, even without an NYT subscription: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/world/europe/germany-stumbling-stones-holocaust-memorial-ban.html?unlocked_article_code=1.FVE.Wjro.cFLW4O8Og3si&smid=url-share
Have to admit I fell for this one. I love a good rebus or three.

I had a colleague in high-school who wouldn't miss a beat if someone stumbled in front of her. "See you after the Fall" or "Have a nice trip" she would say in her very wry and polite British way. Even if I was the one who stumbled, I couldn't help but laugh. It's very nice to have this puzzle remind me of her. Also very nice to see Gay TALESE yet again in a puzzle – like Norman Mailer, a journalism powerhouse. Here he is in a great interview from this past August, looking dapper at 94 – https://www.cbsnews.com/video/tales-from-gay-talese/ Elsewhere in the grid, I smiled when I saw AT SEA. Just yesterday I used it in speaking to someone over the phone as I pointed out that one month had elapsed and I still hadn't yet the answer I needed. "I'm AT SEA here," I said as I wondered if the person on the other end of the line was also a NYT xword solver. Maybe she was. She knew exactly what I meant. She even apologized for my being AT SEA! This was a very pleasant puzzle to solve and the rebuses made it that much better. Its accessibility might even possibly get beginners to fall in love with twists and turns and wouldn't that be something! Thank you, Ms. Singer, for a mighty fine solving trip!

Loved this puzzle! I thought I’d breeze through it after figuring out the rebus, but the stumbling blocks still managed to trip me up for a while - i had GIVE(SLIP)SERVICE for ages, and couldn’t for the life of me figure out the problem. The downs were no help either as i had ‘new’ instead of SAN for the US cities (which admittedly was a stab in the dark, as im not american!). Eventually ended up checking the column to figure out my mistake on the rebus, and it all fell into place from there!
not a bad puzzle, but 16A. is the worst clue and answer i’ve ever seen.

This was so much fun. I knew there were rebuses, and it was a triumphant aha moment when the third one clicked, and I could go back and fill in the other two. Only a little tidying up after that and the puzzle took a bow.

We are so lucky to have entertaining puzzles created by such clever people. They make my day, every day.  Thank you, Ms Singer, for your quartet of constructions. I'm looking forward to No.5.

A Gathering of Clouds was an ENIGMA to me, especially since I was not familiar with that spelling of the Indian tribe. Oh, well. The rest of the puzzle was quite enjoyable, though i think younger people and newer solvers may have trouble with some of the names. By coincidence, my cousins went to see Mozart's Cosi fan TUTTe at the Metropolitan Opera this evening compliments of the NYC/Met Opera ticket giveaway. Here's the overture, in which our old crossword friend, the oboe, and the other woodwinds are highlighted. https://youtu.be/AEramVQ3_Xw?si=rBmZSzClWmAF_RGe

Loved it, and fast Thursday time (for me). My local farm market still swipes my card with the magnetic strip. Now I have to go look at my other cards to see if that strip is gone. Last letter to fall was the T in tutti and Lumet.
Fun!
Took me embarrassingly long to figure out PROFS when that's my own job ::facepalm:: Maybe my subconscious just didn't want to remember the grading pile waiting for me...
Enjoyed it!

What a weird puzzle. The theme was very easy to get, and I found most of the clueing to be extremely direct.

However, then there was the triple natick of the salsa singer, the writer and the Chicago exchange - my only way out of that was with lookups. I didn't get the clue for EST, either, so there was a fourth unknown.

Also, the NE corner was incomparably more difficult for me that the rest of the grid. I managed to resolve it without lookups, but it was a close call. Initially I only had FOCI and the -IANCE of the themed entry there. As I was about to begin revealing entries, PROFS dawned on me. Then I somehow remembered PAIUTE. That gave me enough crosses for DRUM KIT and OINK. Crosses gave me REAMS. It confused me - I don't really understand the clue or how it relates to the entry.

AEIOU... Have any of you typed that in just from its clue, without multiple crosses? Honest question. I first heard of AEIOU in the context of these puzzles, and spotting it does not come intuitively to me (also, in Polish, y is always a vowel). 

SUET as food for woodpeckers was revealed by crosses, only. I had no idea those birds eat anything else than bugs and worms. Apparently people feed them seeds and suet (słonina) in winter Poland, too, but I'm not a bird person so I didn't know it.

I admit your pledge of allegiance has always freaked me out. Over here people were made to publicly recite such things only under totalitarianism. The theocratic mention of God is disturbing in itself.

I ultimately enjoyed the puzzle a lot, but for quite a while I was done in by 17A.  I was sure it referred to the Pledge of Allegiance, but that clearly didn't fit. However, PLEDGE "to the flag" fit perfectly!  I held on to that for far too long before caving in to look for a rebus.

That clouds clue should never have made it to print.

Fine puzzle otherwise. Not much of a Thursday though.

Well, I'm a newbie and this is my first Thursday without any lookups, gold star. Yea! I could use some ABBA or CELIA Cruz to celebrate! Thank you for the music! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0dcbw4IEY5w
The gathering clouds clue is not that great. This is not really why I want to do crosswords...
Why when I complete a puzzle, it doesn’t show as completed? Says I still have clues missing ! Has happened in the past, as well as today.

Missed the solve on this one. Couple of US-centric answers got the better of me.

Whenever I see tribe and the answer isn't 'ute', I'm at sea! So profs, paiute, and foci did it (I had loci so couldn't infer 😬).

I also really must start remembering 'lumet'. It has popped up more than once.
First puzzle in a long while.  Relatively straightforward  for a Thursday, but I enjoyed it.  Thanks to the constructor!
Woodpeckers eat bugs.

[You won't get dirty growing plants this way]




HY(DROP)ONICS

I FELL quickly onto the rebus with the straight forward pledge of allegiance. My only stumbling block was the crossing of Celia with TAlese. Fun puzzle. Would have liked one more rebus,  but I guess I'm happy enough.
I'm always happy to see a rebus, but I wouldn't have minded less direct cluing.
Ugh. Another lost gold due to two unknown squares. CELIA/TALESE and LUMET/TUTTI. Oh well. Guess I should have taken a music class in school. Nice puzzle though. The rebus was cute.

This theme has never been done before (I’ve checked), and it’s so perfect – stumbles in blocks – so crossword iconic, you’d think someone would have come up with it before.  But no, and high credit to Jill for seeing it first.

But then it had to be brought to fruition, and this was done masterfully.  

It’s a tight theme – there aren’t many good synonyms for “stumble” that are short enough for rebuses.  

Then you have to find phrases to embed them in, where these three words don’t have their “stumble” meaning. FALL, for instance, doesn’t mean “stumble” in PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE.   

Jill not only found them, but they are colorful, and with letter counts that fit grid symmetry.  It's uber-tough to make that happen.

And here’s the kicker.  Those three non-revealer theme answers bring sweet freshness to the box.  All of them are Times debut answers!

So, wow, Jill.  This was a gem of a theme in concept and execution, and its beauty beautified my day.  Thank you!

I continue my crusade against unmarked rebuses. 

This was a fun one, and clever without being cute about it or straying into the obtuse, and a very well-constructed puzzle! However, I still think that there should at least be an option for folks to toggle a setting that outlines rebus squares and explains what they are at the beginning of a puzzle where they are present, at the cost of a streak in the same way a checked square or word does now. 

A feature that explains the most opaque crossword convention to the uninitiated while being totally optional and preserving the integrity of a streak would strike a good middle ground, and would not be particularly difficult to write into the existing codebase. The result? Better solvers across the board, and more fun for everybody!

Well, no ENIGMA for me today. Seemed much too gently clued for a Thursday, especially in light of the simplicity and minimality of the rebus theme.

That said, I knew almost all the proper nouns today. Perhaps today's puzzle was more challenging to those who were less fortunate in this regard.

“This is a rebus crossword, in which…”

Closes app. 

Next.

Fun puzzle with an easily discernible rebus aspect, since PLEDGEOFALLEGIANCE was so obvious.

My downfall was the alternate possible spelling of GAIA/GAeA, since I had never heard of the vertical name.

New Thursday record, but I’m not proud of it - the gimmick was easy to suss out and not especially clever, while the cluing was very straightforward. This wasn’t a Thursday puzzle, it was a Monday puzzle with rebuses.  Oh well, on to Friday.

Good puzzle for Latinists, with EST, FOCI (look on any used car lot, and your bound to find several Ford Focī), and TOGA: Fun fact--those little loops in the drapery were known as "sinuses" ("sinūs" in Latin), and were convenient for carrying spare denariī, love letters to one's mistress (written in elegiac couplets, natch), and, of course, tyrannicidal daggers--"ET TU?"

Speaking of tyrants and kings, I suppose, we can add T. REX, and even the eye-scratching OPUSES: although musicians will causally use it, the correct plural is "operas," which comes up in scholarly editions of collected works, as in *The Opera Omnia of Maurice Ravel," which includes his obscure "Concerto for Drum-Kit and Orchestra"--the tutti section mm. 1-65 contains some of 
Ravel's most brilliant writing!

The Earth Goddess has returned from her [TRIP] to Italy, and resumed her preferred spelling.

Suet!

Whatever made you stumble, trip, or fall. 
Call 1800LAWYERUP.


Or less litigiously: kind of a Lego-themed puzzle today, eh parents of toddlers?
Reel-ly fun, staggeringly clever puzzle.  Love Thursdays!
I have to agree with those who found this disappointing for a Thursday. Rather simplistic clueing with way too obvious answers that resulted in a puzzle that lacked the usual Thursday challenge.

I liked that in 17A and 27A, the rebus solution spanned two words: "oFALLegiance" and "paySLIP."  It made it more challenging to solve.  I wish the same rebus trick had been used for 44A, where the rebus was just a single word: STRIPE. Loved the puzzle, though.

An odd mix of straightforward (rebus theme) and a few tricky crosses (31D/39A, 58D/65A) had me chewing the metaphorical pencil end. I’ve read TALISE Gay, but struggled to remember the correct spelling.
I confidently entered Loci and Ants at 12/13D. While the Greater Speckled Woodpecker here eats SUET from our Winter bird tables, the more Common Green exclusively dines on the above mentioned bugs from the lawn (other insects I’m sure are available). I’ve never seen a Green on the feeders, so discounted that as a possible answer. That’s me told. 
Again, with the bravado of misplaced confidence I put Bizet for RAVEL, giving me L-Z for the British endearment. Dear gods, you can’t mean LIZ?? The disastrous, thankfully very short lived tenure of Ms Truss as PM?? Phew. Was happy to amend my error.
I know it’s been mentioned by others (non US types) here, but yes, I also find the custom of reciting a daily PLEDGE very odd and distinctly unsettling. It feels very 1984 to this European. I’m sure there are plenty of things we do that seem odd to a non Brit, so I’m not trying to take any moral high ground here, just that particular custom feels a tad uncanny valley.

Off to check the Alpacas while the visiting Lab is out for a walk. They don’t seem too traumatised by yesterday’s dog invasion/vet visit. Need to keep an eye on them for a couple of days though, as the Bluetongue vaccine isn’t technically registered for Camelids, but it’s the only one out there.
For the first time since I started doing these a few months ago, I got all the rebuses without looking at any hints.

The correct answer for [Woodpecker food] should be EAVE, according to my Partner, given the way they attack our cottage Up North. I could quote some of his more colorful comments about woodpeckers, but the comments would not post, as the emus would side with the woodpeckers.
A bit easy for a Thursday but that means that I managed to get it with no clues or lookups, so Im not complaining.

Clever Thursday puzzle. Enjoyable workout, but I just stuck in a couple of places and couldn't quite work it out. No big deal - that's just me. And.. puzzle find. A Tuesday from June 14, 2016 by Tracy Gray. Four theme answers, straightforwardly clued, though two of them were not familiar to me: EBOLAZAIRE EMILIANOZAPATA EDZWICK EROGENOUSZONES And then the 'reveal,' which was clued as a 'hint' to the theme answers: EASYDOESIT Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=6/14/2016&h=23a Adios ....
Maybe there’s some excuse for having the same goddess twice in a week and spelling the name differently but it’s still stupid.
“Feature of gathering clouds” is such a stupid clue. Otherwise good puzzle.

I just started doing these puzzles recently.

I hate them. They are not crossword puzzles. They are crossphrase puzzles and gimmick puzzles with foolish robot interjections and exhortations.

Those are my cross words of parting!
i hate the rebus, I skip any puzzles with one
Shockingly easy Thursday. C’mon NYT, give us a challenge.

Oh, goody -- a rebus!!!

In fact, I didn't get this at PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE/BEFALL, though both answers befuddled me and I certainly should have.  I got it at PAYS LIP SERVICE TO/SLIP-ONS -- at which point I was able to see the FALL in PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE in my head, without looking at the grid.  And it was so nice to have BEFALL -- which is the answer I had wanted all along for "happen to."

Couldn't guess the revealer in advance -- though I did try to think of one.

I expected the credit card answer to be MAGNETIC STRIP instead of MAGNETIC STRIPE.  Look, I just insert them and then they do their thing, whatever it is.  I don't need to know the inner workings of the credit card as long as it's giving me credit.

The only CRUZes I know are Ted and Penelope.

Did I actually meet Gay TALESE once or did I just see him sitting in a chair in an editor's office I entered?  Did I say anything to him?  Don't remember -- I just know he was quite attractive.  I did have frequent phone contact with his wife Nan who was editor at Random House.  (Don't remember why, though.)

It's hard to think of TREX as a "king" rather than a mere beast, but we do now have a wannabe  king who shares many of TREX's less-attractive qualities.

Give me a rebus and I'm happy.  Even with the clue for AEIOU and the animated series KIM Possible.  Nice embedding of three different forms of STUMBLING

Done with pleasure in half my average Thursday time (though not quite as fast as Thurs. 8/06/26).

I'm reminded of a wise aphorism that I believe was original to a friend of mine in grad school; to wit:

Don't let your milestones be STUMBLING BLOCKS.
Far too many proper nouns IMO. Especially the crossing of TALESE, CELIA, and LUMET LUV RAVEL. Crossword puzzles should be more deduction and less trivia than this one. Theme was very easy too…

Nice theme today.  I knew there was going to be a REBUS for the PAY LIP SERVICE answer then once I got to the revealer they all fell into place.  It helped that the actual REBUS clues weren't very hard so you knew there was a rebus there the moment the obvious answer didn't quite fit.

There was a couple Naticky areas.  Like CELIA crossed with TALESE and MERC, and I've never heard of a TAT of ink.

Also it was a bit mean to have an answer GAIA a few days after an answer GAEA for the same clue when the I crossed a children's show nobody who wasn't a kid or a parent of a young kid when it was on would know about.

Good morning! Got the FALL rebus pretty quick. Then thought it was going to be something to do with seasons, but got the hang of it.
Had a moment with MAGNETICSTRIPE, because I thought it was going to be "strip", and of course the only way for it to fit would be as a plural, and the clue wasn't plural.....yada, yada.
I'm over it! Nice Thursday puzzle.

The three themers had a quaint old-timey feel for me. I have hardly used a plastic credit card in at least 3 years. And PAYSLIPSERVICE feels like its something my dad would have said. I am not sure my thirtyish son even knows what it means. Oh, and who can forget back when it was the *flag* one was required to PLEDGE ALLEGIANCE to and not...ah never mind.
I thought that I had learned a new phrase today until I read Wordplay. I initially read the answer to [Expresses support without meaning it] as Pay Slip Service. Oh well.
Tough to sae.

really liked the puzzle and theme aside from the 2 big naticks:
TALESE x MERC x CELIA

But it was all educated guessing for the proper nouns. I also hit a roadblock at the crossings of Italian music term, a director, British slang, and French composer.

Still managed a clean solve! Chewy enough for me, and if all the answers were in my wheelhouse, it just wouldn't be any fun. Fun theme too, I got the rebus immediately but was expecting seasons, not spills. Nicely done!
Liked it a lot Jill. I'm a fan of rebuses and yours were very good. Two thumbs up 👍👍

Regarding the “Features of gathering clouds” clue, like most I wasn’t thrilled by it, but this sort of clue does pop up occasionally, so I give it a pass. What bothered me more about this clue though is that  I feel like “features” should have been singular. I know that AEIOU consists of multiple letters, but the appearance of them in order in a word or phrase is a singular feature.

I know that’s a tiny nit and I’m not saying the clue was wrong, I just think it would have been better in the singular. Is it just me?

It’s also an autological word: “Supervocalic” is supervocalic.
